findings.issue_text: services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/protocol/oidc/encode/DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider.java:74 — [confidence 100; P2; blocking] `if (encodedContext.length() != 6)` rejects every token emitted for a custom grant following OAuth2GrantTypeFactory.java:30's documented `3-letters shortcut`, because registration and encoding accept arbitrary shortcut lengths while decoding requires exactly two grant characters, so the public grant-factory contract produces tokens the paired decoder cannot read.

adjudication_records.issue_text: services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/protocol/oidc/encode/DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider.java:74 — [confidence 100; P2; blocking] `if (encodedContext.length() != 6)` rejects every token emitted for a custom grant following OAuth2GrantTypeFactory.java:30's documented `3-letters shortcut`, because registration and encoding accept arbitrary shortcut lengths while decoding requires exactly two grant characters, so the public grant-factory contract produces tokens the paired decoder cannot read.

adjudication.rationale: The finding identifies a real inconsistency in the code. Looking at the diff: OAuth2GrantTypeFactory.java:30 documents 'usually like 3-letters shortcut' but the actual implementations use 2-letter shortcuts (e.g., 'ac', 'cc', 'rt', 'ci', 'dg', etc.). The decoder at DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider.java:74 checks `if (encodedContext.length() != 6)` expecting exactly 6 characters total (2 for sessionType + 2 for tokenType + 2 for grantType). The documentation says '3-letters' but implementations use 2-letters, and the decoder enforces 2-letter grant shortcuts. If someone follows the documented '3-letters' guidance, their tokens would fail to decode. However, all built-in implementations correctly use 2-letter shortcuts, so this is more of a documentation/contract inconsistency than a runtime bug for existing code. The finding overstates the severity - existing grants work fine, but the documentation is misleading.

adjudication_records.issue_text: services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/protocol/oidc/encode/DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.java:113 — [confidence 100; P2; blocking] The late-registration path's `grantsByShortcuts.put(shortcut, grantType);` bypasses postInit's uniqueness check, so deploying a new grant with the existing `cc` shortcut overwrites the reverse mapping while retaining client_credentials in the forward mapping and makes both previously issued and new client-credentials tokens decode as the newly deployed grant.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies a real issue. In postInit(), there's a validation check that throws if grantsByShortcuts.size() != grantsToShortcuts.size(), which catches duplicate shortcuts at startup. However, the getShortcutByGrantType() and getGrantTypeByShortcut() methods (lines 103-137) handle late-registration of new grants deployed after startup. These methods directly put new entries into the maps without any uniqueness validation. If a new grant is deployed with a shortcut that already exists (e.g., 'cc'), the code at line 113 does `grantsByShortcuts.put(shortcut, grantType)` which overwrites the existing mapping, while line 114 adds a new entry to grantsToShortcuts. This creates an inconsistent state where the forward map has the new grant for 'cc' but the reverse map has both the old and new grants pointing to 'cc'. This would cause tokens issued with client_credentials to decode incorrectly.
